content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a common condition in children. These infections occur when bacteria invade the urinary tract, specifically the bladder (resulting in a lower tract infection) or the kidneys (resulting in an upper tract infection). Upper tract infections, such as pyelonephritis, are characterized by symptoms including abdominal pain, loin tenderness, fever, anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, and malaise. Lower tract infections, such as cystitis, typically present with lower abdominal or suprapubic pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. In younger children, the clinical signs are often nonspecific, making it challenging to distinguish between upper and lower tract infections. By the age of five, approximately 8% of girls and 2% of boys will have experienced a UTI. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment are critical to minimizing the morbidity associated with this condition. Causes of UTIs UTIs can be classified into two main types: bladder infections (cystitis) and kidney infections (pyelonephritis). Cystitis causes pain and swelling in the bladder, while pyelonephritis is a more severe condition that can potentially damage the kidneys. The most common causative organism of UTIs in children is Escherichia coli (E. coli). Other pathogens include: Klebsiella (the second most common cause), Proteus species, Enterobacter species, Enterococcus species, Citrobacter species, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and Candida albicans (in certain cases). Mechanical Predisposing Factors The most common predisposing factor for recurrent UTIs is vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), a condition where urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureters or kidneys. Other mechanical factors include urinary obstruction. Diagnostic Imaging Recommendations The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends specific imaging studies following an initial febrile UTI in children under two years of age. These include: Renal and bladder ultrasonography to detect anatomical abnormalities, Voiding cystourethrography (VCUG) or radionuclide cystography if ultrasonography reveals findings such as hydronephrosis, scarring, or high-grade VUR. Treatment Goals The primary objectives of UTI treatment in children are: 1. Elimination of the acute infection, 2. Prevention of complications, and 3. Reduction of renal damage. Diagnostic and Treatment Guidelines Diagnostic ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder is essential to identify any anatomical abnormalities. VCUG is indicated only if ultrasonography reveals concerning findings such as hydronephrosis, scarring, or high-grade VUR. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting microscopy or culture results, as this could be harmful. Avoid the Following Routine diagnostic imaging for all children with a first UTI is not recommended. Prophylactic antimicrobial therapy to prevent febrile recurrent UTIs is not advised. Surgical correction of minor functional abnormalities or moderate VUR is generally unnecessary.
